title: Enterprise Self-Heal Automation Playbook
author: Leah Kim
body:
Summary

This playbook describes the standardized approach Redwood Customer Success (CS) and Support teams use to implement, validate, and operate enterprise self-heal automation for customer production incidents. Self-heal automation refers to fully automated remediation actions that are safe to run without human approval when a monitored condition maps to a validated remediation recipe. The goal is to reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), lower toil for on-call engineers, and preserve customer SLAs while maintaining auditability and revertibility.

When to use this playbook

- Enterprise customers with a Dedicated or Private deployment where the customer has agreed to automated remediation in their onboarding contract.
- Routine, well-understood failure classes where automated remediation has been tested end-to-end and has a clear rollback path.
- Situations where automation improves availability and cost predictability (e.g., autoscaling policies, model switchover, cache invalidation, connector restarts).

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: networking reconnections, connector/ingest restarts, GK (gateway) route fallback, model variant switchovers, KV-cache warmup, automated quota adjustments with throttled rollback.
- Non-goal: Automated changes to customer data schema, irreversible data migrations, or actions that materially change billing without human sign-off.

Roles and ownership

- Customer Success (CS): negotiates automation consent, documents high-level workflows in the customer onboarding packet, approves business-level safety constraints.
- Support (Tier 1/2): triage alerts, confirm automation mapping, escalate when automation does not resolve incident.
- Platform Reliability (Eng-SRE): implements and maintains automation recipes and ensures telemetry coverage and safety gates.
- Customer Oncall: receives notices of automatic remediation and can request immediate pause/rollback.

Alerting and detection (signals)

Primary signals that may trigger self-heal automation:

1) Service health metrics exceeding thresholds
   - API error rate > 5% over 3 minutes AND p95 latency > 1.2s on critical routes
   - Model inference tail latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes
2) Capacity saturation
   - GPU pool utilization > 92% sustained for 10 minutes
   - Pod eviction rate > 1/min for 3 minutes
3) External integrations failing
   - Upstream telemetry forwarding HTTP 5xx > 2% for 5 minutes
4) Data pipeline stalls
   - Connector lag > 30 minutes and backlog growth > 10% over 15 minutes

Every trigger must map to a single canonical alert ID (format: cs/selfheal/{customer}/{alert-type}) and include the following context: customer_id, tenant_type (hosted/dedicated/private), service, region, recent_error_snippet, and current_runbook_version.

Safety gates and preconditions

Automation must not run unless all the following are true:

- Customer has opted-in in the onboarding contract and the opt-in record exists in the CS portal.
- The active SLOs for the customer are known and automation allowed for the SLO class.
- At least one recent successful telemetry heartbeat from the effected service in the last 5 minutes.
- No active incident labeled "major-outage" for the same customer.
- Automation run quota for the customer has not been exhausted (default 6 runs / 24 hours).

Automation recipes and examples

Each automation recipe is a small documented unit with: trigger definition, preconditions, exact steps, rollback procedure, runbook link, required RBAC role, and audit metadata. Examples below are canonical recipes we use as templates.

Recipe: connector-restart-with-backoff
- Trigger: connector HTTP 5xx > 3% for 5 minutes OR connector crashlooping > 3 restarts / 10 minutes
- Preconditions: opt-in, recent heartbeat, automation quota available
- Steps (automated):
  1. Create incident stub and link to customer's CS record.
  2. Annotate monitoring event with automation_run_id and start timestamp.
  3. Graceful restart of connector (POST /customer/{id}/connectors/{id}/actions/restart?mode=graceful) with timeout 45s.
  4. Wait for successful healthcheck: GET /health/connectors/{id} (retry 3x @ 10s).
  5. If healthcheck passes, warm cache prefetch job (async).
  6. Close incident stub with resolution code AUTOMATED_RESTART_SUCCESS.
- Rollback: If healthcheck fails after step 3, perform a forced restart and escalate to Support Tier 2.
- Audit: All steps produce structured events to /events/selfheal with policy_id and automation_run_id.

Recipe: model-variant-failover
- Trigger: model container OOM or degraded token throughput > 40% for 10 minutes
- Preconditions: compatible fallback model available for customer's deployment, model cost tier alignment checked
- Steps:
  1. Mark route read-only for new non-essential low-priority requests for 60s.
  2. Gradually shift 10% traffic to fallback variant and monitor quality/regression metrics over 5 minutes.
  3. If quality regression <= 3% on customer eval prompts and latency improves, continue rollout to 100% with incremental steps (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%).
  4. Notify customer and CS with rollout timeline and telemetry links.
- Rollback: Immediate rollback to pinned model if regression > 3% at any step.

Implementation patterns and safe primitives

- Idempotent actions: All APIs called by automations must be idempotent or have safe detect-and-noop semantics.
- Circuit breaker: Automations include a local circuit that prevents repeated runs against the same target if failure rate does not drop after 3 attempts.
- Scoped throttling: Rate-limit automation actions per customer and per resource to prevent cascading failures.
- Audit trail: Structured JSON logs for every automation run (fields: automation_run_id, policy_id, initiator=automation, preconditions, steps, outcomes, timestamps, owner_contact).

Change control and deployment process for recipes

1. Author drafts recipe as a PR in infra-selfheal repo. PR must include unit tests, integration tests that run in the staging harness, and a safety checklist.
2. Reviewer from Eng-SRE + CS reviews. At least one security review if the recipe touches credentials or billing APIs.
3. Merge to canary namespace. Run automated canary for 72h against internal staging tenants.
4. After canary, run a small customer pilot (customer consented) for 7 days. Collect metrics.
5. Publish recipe and enable policy with default disabled. CS will opt-in customers per onboarding workflows.

Testing and validation

- Unit tests: validate precondition checks and idempotency.
- Integration tests: run simulated alert flows in the staging harness with injected failures.
- Chaos tests: periodically run chaos scenarios (connector failures, model OOMs) in a controlled environment.
- Observability: every test run writes to a test-results index and dashboard with pass/fail and measured MTTR impact.

Runbook: manual handoff if automation fails

1. Alert hits Support Tier 1 with automation_run_id. Tier 1 examines automation logs and outcome.
2. If automation indicates escalation, escalate to Tier 2 with all artifacts and recent logs.
3. Tier 2 can trigger manual remediation steps defined in recipe replaced with the suffix "-manual" (e.g., connector-restart-with-backoff-manual).
4. If remediation is not possible, initiate incident bridge and follow incident process in oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks.

Customer onboarding checklist for self-heal

- Confirm opt-in consent documented in contract and entered in CS portal.
- Capture customer SLOs and forbidden actions (e.g., no automated model changes).
- Define allowed automation classes (networking, connectors, autoscaling, model failover) and list explicit exclusions.
- Validate telemetry coverage: API, model, and infra metrics mapped and test alerts fired in staging.
- Schedule pilot window and agree on rollback SLA.

KPIs and QBR evidence

- Primary KPIs: automated MTTR reduction (target: 35% lower MTTR vs manual), automation success rate (target >= 85%), false positive initiations (target <= 5% of runs).
- QBR artifacts: automation run summary (CSV), incident reduction chart, example case studies, telemetry dashboards links, and an agreed action list for tuning policies.

Safety checklist before enabling automation for a customer

- [ ] Contract opt-in present and timestamped
- [ ] Telemetry heartbeat validated in prod -> last 5 minutes
- [ ] Run quota and circuit settings reviewed with CS
- [ ] Emergency pause playbook shared with customer oncall
- [ ] Customer acceptance test (CAT) executed in canary environment

Example webhook payload (automation start event)

{\n  "automation_run_id": "arun-20260112-9b7f",\n  "policy_id": "policy-connector-restart-v2",\n  "customer_id": "cust-4512",\n  "trigger": "connector_http_5xx_threshold",\n  "preconditions": ["opt_in", "heartbeat_ok"],\n  "initiator": "automation",\n  "timestamp": "2026-01-12T18:22:11Z"\n}

CLI example: pause automation for a customer

# Pause automation for cust-4512 for 1 hour
redwoodctl customers automation pause --customer cust-4512 --duration 60m --reason "customer requested pause for maintenance"

Operational play: emergency pause and rollback

- CS or oncall may invoke redwoodctl to pause automation immediately; this action must generate a notification to CS leads and the customer oncall.
- To rollback a model switchover: redwoodctl routeset rollback --customer cust-4512 --from variant-b --to variant-a --force \\n  (Allowed only if manual approval present or regression threshold exceeded.)
